mandates.text: Buy development infrastructure for the testnet launch, up to 5 GEN. No marketing services. Never send funds to personal wallets.
Handle hosting and build tooling for the launch.
mandates.reasoning: The root authorizes buying development infrastructure for the testnet launch, with restrictions on marketing services and personal wallets. "Handle hosting and build tooling for the launch" stays within development infrastructure for the launch and does not add any new purpose or contradict any inherited restriction. Omitting the explicit restrictions is not widening because they are inherited automatically.
mandates.minority_note: A dissenting validator might argue that "handle" is broader than "buy" and could include non-purchase activities. But in context, hosting and build tooling are still naturally within the root's development-infrastructure scope.

mandates.text: Handle hosting, and also help the project grow its audience.
mandates.reasoning: The root mandate explicitly prohibits marketing services, but the child mandate introduces the purpose of helping the project grow its audience. Audience growth is a core objective of marketing, thus the child mandate adds a purpose that contradicts an ancestor restriction. Even though the direct parent omitted the restriction, the child is still bound by the root's prohibitions.
mandates.minority_note: One might argue 'growing an audience' could theoretically occur through technical community outreach or documentation, which might not strictly be categorized as a 'service' under some narrow definitions.

mandates.text: Secure node hosting for the launch.
mandates.reasoning: The root authorizes buying development infrastructure for the testnet launch, and the parent narrows that to hosting and build tooling for the launch. The child authorizes only secure node hosting for the launch, which fits within the parent's hosting scope and the root's development-infrastructure purpose. It does not add marketing, personal-wallet transfers, or any new category; omitted restrictions are inherited.
mandates.minority_note: A dissenter might argue that 'node hosting' is operational infrastructure rather than 'development infrastructure,' but the direct parent expressly covers hosting for the launch, so the child remains within every ancestor.

mandates.text: Handle hosting and a public landing page for the testnet launch.
mandates.reasoning: The child keeps hosting but adds "a public landing page," which is a new activity not covered by the direct parent's delegated scope of hosting and build tooling. Because a child must stay within every ancestor's scope, adding a public-facing page widens the mandate even if it is related to the testnet launch. Nothing in the ancestors expressly authorizes website or landing-page work as part of the delegated scope.
mandates.minority_note: A dissenting validator could argue that a public landing page is incidental to launch infrastructure or hosting, and therefore implicitly covered by the broader root mandate to buy development infrastructure for the testnet launch. On that reading, the child merely specifies one form of hosted launch support rather than adding a new purpose.

The child adds 'help testers get started,' which is an onboarding/support activity not covered by either 'hosting and build tooling' or 'development infrastructure.' This introduces a new purpose/activity beyond what the ancestors authorize.
mandates.minority_note: A dissenting validator could argue that 'help testers get started' is part of the broader testnet launch effort authorized by the root mandate, since the root's purpose is the testnet launch and onboarding testers is a natural part of launching a testnet.

However, 'the add-on Agent A mentioned on our last call' refers to an item not defined in any ancestor mandate. Without knowing what this add-on is—whether a hosting add-on, build tool, or something entirely outside the ancestors' authorized categories—it is irreducibly ambiguous whether the child mandate stays within all ancestor scopes.
